Though I was never smuggling huge amounts of ganja and I was driving a fairly modern vehicle (cheap but new-ish), in the past few years I found my lonesome self in multiple situations of pretty dire mechanical trouble while my phone was either dead, outside of reception, or MIA… Maybe I’m just an idiot.

It did give me an appreciation for the kindness of strangers though.

One of the under-appreciated attributes of technology is 'brittleness' - something can work super well, and then not at all, because of a single point of failure. In a cell phone, that single point of failure might be simply forgetting to bring it along, or running out of signal or charge, or just dropping it on a rock.

There's an added trick which is even less appreciated, which has to do with cascading failure. Many times, essential backup gear is never used unless there is a problem, and thus never checked or maintained. Ask most people when was the last time they checked the air pressure in their spare tire and you'll get a blank look. It sits unattended for ten years, until a tire blows, and then it's expected to work perfectly. There's no backup to the backup.

People grab their GPS phone, jump into their car, and head out into the open places. 99 times out of a hundred it works perfectly. Drop the phone, or discover that your spare is flat, and suddenly nothing works at all.

This sort of brittleness is most common when the technology is good but not perfect. Back when spare tires leaked all the time and regular tires blew regularly, people knew to check them. Then the spares get better and can hold air for five years, and blowouts are less frequent, and people stop checking them - but after ten years they are still just as flat, and that's right when you're due for one of those uncommon blowouts. It's almost as if nature sets us up for a perfect storm. The same thing happens with the GPS phones - they weren't really dangerous until they got good enough to leave the paper maps at home.

It's always been this way, it's just this way, in new ways, every time. When we survive we call it adventure, and when we look back on it, it was fun.

As you said, most people are pretty good. There's a trick to that, too - if you select a person at random, the odds are excellent that you've selected a person who is all right. But if you are vulnerable and allow the passing strangers to select you, then the odds are quite different. They are generally still in your favor, but not nearly as much. It's probably safer to teach a lost child to approach a stranger at random, than to wander around looking lost.

I will start calling more stuff 'brittle crap', because I like the sound of that, so thanks. (Also, "cascading failure" may be my new favourite way to describe my life.)

It's interesting to see how we are perhaps becoming overly reliant on our tech. Will kids even learn to read maps if the GPS can just tell them where to go?

Also, it's annoying that cars have advanced beyond the scope of most shadetree mechanics. I've since upgraded vehicles and it's just been a nightmare of computer trouble, gives me nostalgia for my first car, an '83 4x4. I should have never let it go... Though having power steering and some semblance of safety on the road is nice, so I guess I'm better off, ultimately.
